lessons.title: يكتب (yaktubu) — the present, for everyone
lessons.gloss: the present for every person — a- for I, ta- for you and she, ya- for he, na- for we, all on the same stem

segments.text: Say "I write". (Aktub.) Then say the Arabic for a sentence and a barber. (Jumla, ḥallāq.)
Chapter thirty-seven gave you the present for one person only: أ at the front means I. A story needs he, she and we as well, and they come from the same front door.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: one stem, four prefixes

segments.text: Keep the stem -ktub- and change the letter in front of it:
أكتب aktubu, I write, تكتب taktubu, you write, يكتب yaktubu, he writes, تكتب taktubu, she writes, نكتب naktubu, we write.
Ta- does two jobs: "you" said to a man, and "she". The sentence around it tells them apart. Said to a woman, "you write" adds -īna at the back, taktubīna, and "they write" adds -ūna, yaktubūna.
The -u at the end is the present's own vowel. At the end of a sentence it is usually dropped, which is why chapter thirty-seven wrote aktub; inside a sentence you will hear it.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the same door on other verbs

segments.text: هي تكتب رسالة. — hiya taktubu risāla — She is writing a letter.
نحن نذهب إلى المدرسة. — naḥnu nadhhabu ilā al-madrasa — We go to school.

Dhahaba gives nadhhabu; qaraʾa gives yaqraʾu, he reads. One present covers "I write" and "I am writing"; English splits what Arabic keeps as one. Huwa is "he", hiya "she", naḥnu "we", and they are often left out, because the prefix already says who.

segments.instruction: aktubu, taktubu, yaktubu, naktubu
"She is writing a letter" — hiya taktubu risāla
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "She is writing a letter" — *hiya taktubu risāla*]

segments.instruction: "He reads a book" — yaqraʾu kitāban
"We go to school" — nadhhabu ilā al-madrasa
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "We go to school" — *nadhhabu ilā al-madrasa*]

segments.instruction: "The actor reads", with the word from chapter two hundred and eighty-one — al-mumaththil yaqraʾu
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "The actor reads", with the word from chapter two hundred and eighty-one — *al-mumaththil yaqraʾu*]

segments.text: Which letter at the front means we? (ن, na-.) And he? (ي, ya-.) Why can تكتب mean two people? (Ta- is "you" and "she": the sentence decides.) Where is the -u dropped? (At the end of a sentence.)

lessons.title: كتبت (katabtu) — the past, person by person
lessons.gloss: the past for every person — the endings -tu, -ta, -ti, -at, -nā, -ū on the stem of kataba

segments.text: Say "we write", then "he writes". (Naktubu, yaktubu.)
You have said qaḍaytu al-ʿuṭla fī al-qarya, "I spent the holiday in the village". That -tu at the back is "I" in the past. Here is the rest of the set.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the endings at the back

segments.text: Kataba, he wrote, is the bare past. Every other person is an ending on the same stem, katab-:
كتبتُ katabtu, I wrote, كتبتَ katabta, you wrote (to a man), كتبتِ katabti, you wrote (to a woman), كتبَ kataba, he wrote, كتبتْ katabat, she wrote, كتبنا katabnā, we wrote, كتبوا katabū, they wrote.
The present put the person at the front; the past puts it at the back.

Without its vowel marks, كتبت spells four of these at once: katabtu, katabta, katabti and katabat. That is why they carry marks here, and why, on an unmarked page, the rest of the sentence tells you who wrote.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: other verbs, and "did not"

segments.text: أمس كتبت رسالة إلى جدتي. — ams katabtu risālatan ilā jaddatī — Yesterday I wrote a letter to my grandmother.
ذهبنا إلى السوق. — dhahabnā ilā as-sūq — We went to the market.
Qaraʾa gives qaraʾtu, I read; dhahaba gives dhahabat, she went. The ا at the end of كتبوا is written and not said.
ما in front makes it "did not": mā katabtu, I didn't write; mā dhahabnā, we didn't go.

segments.instruction: katabtu, katabta, katabti, kataba, katabat, katabnā, katabū
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *katabtu, katabta, katabti, kataba, katabat, katabnā, katabū*]

segments.instruction: "Yesterday I wrote a letter" — ams katabtu risālatan
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "Yesterday I wrote a letter" — *ams katabtu risālatan*]

segments.instruction: "We went to the market", then "we didn't go" — dhahabnā ilā as-sūq, mā dhahabnā
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "We went to the market", then "we didn't go" — *dhahabnā ilā as-sūq*, *mā dhahabnā*]

segments.instruction: "They came back to the house" — rajaʿū ilā al-manzil
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "They came back to the house" — *rajaʿū ilā al-manzil*]

segments.instruction: "The engineer read the letter" — al-muhandis qaraʾa ar-risāla
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "The engineer read the letter" — *al-muhandis qaraʾa ar-risāla*]

segments.text: Where does the past mark the person? (At the back.) "She wrote"? (Katabat.) "We wrote"? (Katabnā.) How many persons can an unmarked كتبت be? (Four: katabtu, katabta, katabti, katabat.) "I didn't go"? (Mā dhahabtu.)

lessons.title: كان (kāna) — was
lessons.gloss: to be (in the past); was — the verb the present leaves out

segments.text: Say "I wrote" and "she wrote". (Katabtu, katabat.)
Now say "I am at the office". (Anā fī al-maktab.) There is no "am" in it: in the present, Arabic sets the two halves side by side. In the past it cannot, and it needs a verb.
كان — kāna — "he was, it was": the past of "to be".
كنت في المكتب أمس. — kuntu fī al-maktab ams — I was at the office yesterday.
كانت جدتي في القرية. — kānat jaddatī fī al-qarya — My grandmother was in the village.

It takes the endings of the lesson before, with one change. Where the ending starts with a consonant, the long ā shrinks to u: kuntu, I was; kunta, kunti, you were; kunnā, we were. Where it does not, the ā stays: kāna, kānat, kānū, they were.

كان (kāna) is built on the native Arabic root k-w-n, "to be, to come into being" (Lane). Lane lists makāna, "a place of being", among the words of the same root. The w of the root is the reason for the two shapes: it surfaces as long ā in kāna and as short u in kuntu.

segments.instruction: kāna, kānat — then kuntu, kunnā
"I was at the office yesterday" — kuntu fī al-maktab ams
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "I was at the office yesterday" — *kuntu fī al-maktab ams*]

segments.instruction: "We were in the restaurant" — kunnā fī al-maṭʿam
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "We were in the restaurant" — *kunnā fī al-maṭʿam*]

segments.instruction: "My grandmother was in the village" — kānat jaddatī fī al-qarya
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "My grandmother was in the village" — *kānat jaddatī fī al-qarya*]

segments.text: What does كان (kāna) mean? ("He was; it was".) "I was"? (Kuntu, with a short u.) "She was"? (Kānat, with a long ā.) Why does the present not need it? (Arabic sets the two halves side by side.)

lessons.title: كان يكتب (kāna yaktubu) — the past that is still running
lessons.gloss: the past still running — kāna in front of the present paints the scene or the habit, and the plain past drops the events into it

segments.text: Say "I was at the office", then "I wrote". (Kuntu fī al-maktab, katabtu.)
Katabtu has an edge: the writing happened, and it is over. A story also needs a past with no edge on it.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: kāna in front of the present

segments.text: Put kāna in its past form, then the present of the verb you mean, both for the same person:
kuntu + aktubu becomes كنت أكتب — kuntu aktubu — I was writing; I used to write.
So kānat taqraʾu, she was reading; kunnā nadhhabu, we used to go. It answers two English shapes. "Was ‑ing": the action was under way. "Used to": it happened again and again.
كنت أمشي إلى المدرسة كل يوم. — kuntu amshī ilā al-madrasa kulla yawm — I used to walk to school every day.
Mā goes in front of kāna: mā kuntu aʿrifu, I didn't know.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the scene, and the event

segments.text: A told story splits its verbs in two. Kāna with the present paints the scene: what was going on. The plain past drops the events into it: what happened.
كنت أقرأ كتابا حينما اتصل صديقي. — kuntu aqraʾu kitāban ḥīnamā ittaṣala ṣadīqī — I was reading a book when my friend phoned.
The reading is scene, still running when the call cuts into it. The call is an event, over in a moment, and ḥīnamā is the joint between them.

segments.instruction: kuntu aktubu, kānat taktubu, kunnā naktubu
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *kuntu aktubu, kānat taktubu, kunnā naktubu*]

segments.instruction: "I used to walk to school every day" — kuntu amshī ilā al-madrasa kulla yawm
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "I used to walk to school every day" — *kuntu amshī ilā al-madrasa kulla yawm*]

segments.instruction: kuntu aqraʾu kitāban ḥīnamā ittaṣala ṣadīqī
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *kuntu aqraʾu kitāban ḥīnamā ittaṣala ṣadīqī*]

segments.instruction: "I didn't know" — mā kuntu aʿrifu
"She was reading a page" — kānat taqraʾu ṣafḥa
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "She was reading a page" — *kānat taqraʾu ṣafḥa*]

segments.text: How do you build "I was writing"? (Kuntu + aktubu: kuntu aktubu.) In the phone sentence, which verb is the scene? (Kuntu aqraʾu, still running.) Which is the event? (Ittaṣala, over in a moment.) Do both verbs agree with the person? (Yes: kunnā naktubu.)

lessons.title: Review — the scene, and what cut into it
lessons.gloss: the present for every person, the past for every person, kāna, and kāna with the present for the scene

segments.text: Say "he writes" for today, then "he wrote" for yesterday. (Yaktubu, kataba.) Then the Arabic for a calculator and a pencil case. (Ḥāsiba, miqlama.)

Four lessons, one stem, and three shapes of it. The present marks the person at the front: aktubu, taktubu, yaktubu, naktubu. The past marks it at the back: katabtu, katabat, katabnā, katabū. And kāna in front of the present gives the past that is still running: kuntu aktubu.
Al-māḍī sets the time:
كنت أعمل في المكتب الأسبوع الماضي. — kuntu aʿmalu fī al-maktab al-usbūʿa al-māḍī — Last week I was working at the office.
And ḥīnamā joins the scene to the event that cut into it:
كانت تكتب قصة حينما جاء أخوها. — kānat taktubu qiṣṣa ḥīnamā jāʾa akhūhā — She was writing a story when her brother came.

segments.instruction: a scene in two — kuntu fī al-maktab. kuntu aktubu.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: a scene in two — *kuntu fī al-maktab. kuntu aktubu.*]

segments.instruction: "Last week I was working at the office" — kuntu aʿmalu fī al-maktab al-usbūʿa al-māḍī
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "Last week I was working at the office" — *kuntu aʿmalu fī al-maktab al-usbūʿa al-māḍī*]

segments.text: After ḥīnamā in a story, which past? (The plain one, the event: jāʾa.) Which past paints the scene? (Kāna with the present.) "We were"? (Kunnā.) "Last week"? (Al-usbūʿ al-māḍī.)
